cards.text: Friend, the prophet Isaiah has a new message from the LORD: a burden against Damascus, the capital of Aram (Isaiah 7:8). I'll be honest, nobody's getting a thank-you card in this one. The LORD opens with what's become of the city.

cards.question: What does the LORD say Damascus has become?

cards.text: Damascus isn't the only place emptied out. The cities of Aroer are forsaken, and all that open space is about to get some new residents.

cards.question: Who moves into the forsaken cities of Aroer?

cards.text: Then the LORD of Hosts says the fortress will disappear from Ephraim, the kingdom whose capital is Samaria (Isaiah 7:9), and the sovereignty from Damascus. Two kingdoms, same bad news.

cards.question: The LORD says what's left of Aram will be like the splendor of which people?
In that day, the LORD says, the splendor of Jacob, Israel's people, will ___.

cards.text: And the fat of his body will waste away. The LORD compares it to a reaper gathering the standing grain with his arm, like someone gleaning heads of grain in the Valley of Rephaim.

cards.question: True or false: After the reaping, the LORD says gleanings will still remain.

cards.text: Then the picture changes to an olive tree that's been beaten. Somebody went at that tree like it was the snooze button.

cards.question: When the beaten olive tree is done, what's left on it?

cards.text: Two or three berries up top, four or five on the fruitful branches. That's my chocolate chip jar after I "taste-test" a batch, and the only suspect has a MUSTACHE.

cards.question: But in that day, people look up. Men will look to their ___ and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel.
True or false: When men turn their eyes to their Maker, they'll keep looking to the altars they made with their own hands.

cards.text: In that day, their strong cities will be like forsaken thickets and summits, abandoned to utter desolation. And the message spells out why.

cards.question: Why is all this coming? The message says, you have ___ the God of your salvation.

cards.text: And failed to remember the Rock of your refuge, too. I spent years forgotten in a junk drawer, friend, but forgetting the God who saves is a darker drawer than mine.
Then a garden picture: delightful plots, cuttings from exotic vines, seed sprouting the very morning it's planted. Somebody's hovering over that garden like I hover over the oven window.

cards.question: True or false: After all that careful planting, the harvest comes in big.

cards.text: Instead, the harvest vanishes on the day of disease and incurable pain. Then the message gets LOUD: many peoples raging like the roaring seas, rumbling like the crashing of mighty waters.

cards.question: True or false: When the LORD rebukes the raging nations, they stand their ground.

cards.text: They flee far away, driven before the wind like chaff on the hills, like tumbleweeds before a gale. All that roaring, and they scatter like the crumbs on my counter when I sneeze.

cards.question: In the evening, sudden terror strikes the raging nations. When are they no more?
The message says this sudden end is the portion of which people?

findings.problem: The question asks whose splendor Aram's remnant will be like, and the answer is the Israelites. Card 5 introduces Ephraim only as 'the kingdom whose capital is Samaria' and never links Ephraim to Israel. Without that link, the baker can't reason from Ephraim to the Israelites, so the pick between Israelites, Egyptians and Babylonians is luck. The link is easy to give (for example, that Ephraim is Israel), so this shouldn't be one of the allowed discovery questions.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The question says 'sudden terror strikes the raging nations.' Isaiah 17:14 only says 'In the evening, there is sudden terror!' and never says who the terror falls on. The card adds a target the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: This is a who question, but the wrong answers 'those who mourn Damascus' and 'those who rebuild Aroer' are made up. They aren't real details from the Bible. Also, the right answer is the only one with the passage's 'us' wording, so it stands out.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.
